caption: "mexican independence day" — 100,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the night Mexico shouts.

Why: September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day, the 216th since a priest named Miguel Hidalgo rang a church bell in Dolores at 2:30 in the morning in 1810 and called the town to arms. On the night of September 15 President Claudia Sheinbaum gave the Grito from the National Palace balcony to more than 300,000 people.

What most people don't know: it is not Cinco de Mayo. May 5 marks one battle against France in 1862. The bell the president rings is Hidalgo's own, moved to the palace in 1896. And nobody knows Hidalgo's exact words; no record survives.
Very simply put: the world's most famous Mexican holiday is the wrong one.

slides.headline: It began with a *church bell* at 2:30 am on September 16, 1810.
slides.sub: Priest Miguel Hidalgo rang it in Dolores, Guanajuato, and called the town to arms.

slides.headline: Cinco de Mayo is a *different war*.
slides.sub: May 5 remembers one battle against the French army in Puebla in 1862, 52 years later.
slides.image: Old iron cannon on a stone rampart overlooking hills at sunrise, cannon in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain stone floor, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: The president rings *Hidalgo's actual bell*.
slides.sub: Porfirio Díaz had it brought from Dolores in 1896 and rang it from the balcony himself. It was cast in 1768.
slides.image: Large bronze bell hanging in an arched stone balcony above a sea of small crowd lights at night, bell in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark, photorealistic, no text, no flags

slides.headline: The shout comes the *night before*, at 11 pm on September 15.
slides.sub: Díaz rang it on the night of September 15, 1896, and the eve stuck. A popular story says he chose it because September 15 was his birthday.

slides.headline: This year's crowd: *more than 300,000* in the Zócalo.
slides.sub: The city's count on September 15, 2026, a record for the ceremony.

slides.headline: The president shouts *21 vivas*.
slides.sub: Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico's first woman president, named women insurgents among the heroes: Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario, Gertrudis Bocanegra.

slides.headline: Nobody knows Hidalgo's *exact words*.
slides.sub: Historians disagree on his exact words. One wrote there are as many versions as there are historians.
slides.image: Antique blank parchment scroll, torn at the edge, on a dark wooden table in candlelight, scroll in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark wood, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: Independence took *11 more years*.
slides.sub: Hidalgo was captured and executed in 1811. Independence came 11 years and 12 days after his shout, on September 28, 1821.
